words.definition: A treatment or solution that cures an illness or corrects a problem.
words.example: Grandma swore that honey and lemon was the best remedy for a sore throat.
words.mnemonic: Remedy contains 'med' as in medicine — the medicine you take to get better.

words.definition: To settle a dispute or find a solution to a problem.
words.example: After hours of heated debate, the two sides finally resolved their argument over the budget.
words.mnemonic: RE + SOLVE — you solve the problem again and again until it is settled for good.

words.definition: To restore friendly relations between people or make conflicting ideas agree.
words.example: After years of silence, the estranged brothers finally reconciled at their mother's funeral.
words.mnemonic: RE + CONCILE (think 'council') — bringing people back to the same council table.

words.definition: Correction of an unfair situation, or compensation given for a wrong.
words.example: The factory workers marched to demand redress for years of unpaid overtime.
words.mnemonic: RE-DRESS — you 'dress' a wound or a wrong a second time to set it right.

words.definition: To correct something wrong or fix a mistake.
words.example: The bank promised to rectify the billing error and refund every extra charge.
words.mnemonic: RECT- means 'right' (Latin rectus, as in 'correct') + -IFY — to make right.

words.definition: To fix or reverse damage, especially to the environment or a deficiency.
words.example: The company spent millions to remediate the soil contaminated by its old factory.
words.mnemonic: RE-MEDI-ATE — apply 'medi' (medicine) to a sick site until it heals.

words.definition: To save something from destruction, loss, or a disaster.
words.example: Divers managed to salvage gold coins from the Spanish galleon that sank centuries ago.
words.mnemonic: Salvage shares its root with 'salvation' — both are about saving from ruin.

words.definition: To repair something broken or torn, or to heal over time.
words.example: She sat by the window mending the torn knee of her son's favorite jeans.
words.mnemonic: Mend is 'amend' with the 'a' knocked off — quietly putting things right.

words.definition: Payment or action made to compensate for harm or a wrong done.
words.example: The peace treaty required the defeated nation to pay reparations to its neighbors.
words.mnemonic: RE + PARATION (hear 'repair') — repairing the damage, often with money.

words.definition: Easing pain or symptoms without curing the underlying cause.
words.example: The new drug was merely palliative, dulling his pain while the disease kept spreading.
words.mnemonic: A 'pall' is a cloak — palliative care throws a cloak over the pain instead of removing it.

words.definition: A single solution supposedly able to cure all ills or fix every problem.
words.example: Politicians pitched the tax cut as a panacea for every economic woe the country faced.
words.mnemonic: PAN- (Greek for 'all') + -ACEA — from Panacea, the Greek goddess who healed all.

words.definition: A state of confusion about what to do in a difficult situation.
words.example: Offered two dream jobs on the very same afternoon, she found herself in a real quandary.
words.mnemonic: Quandary sounds like 'wonder-y' — you keep wondering which way to turn.

words.definition: A hard choice between two options, often both undesirable.
words.example: He faced the classic dilemma of telling a painful truth or offering a kind lie.
words.mnemonic: DI- (Greek 'two') + -LEMMA ('proposition') — two propositions, and neither is good.

words.definition: A difficult, unpleasant, or embarrassing situation that is hard to escape.
words.example: Locked out in the pouring rain, she called a locksmith to get her out of the predicament.
words.mnemonic: Predicament — 'predict-a-ment'; it's so tangled you can't predict a way out.

words.definition: A dangerous, sad, or difficult condition someone is stuck in.
words.example: The documentary spotlighted the plight of refugees fleeing the war-torn border region.
words.mnemonic: Plight rhymes with 'blight' — both name something that has gone badly wrong.

words.definition: A situation in which no progress can be made because opposing sides refuse to yield.
words.example: After twelve hours of talks, the union and management hit an impasse and went home.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'im-pass' — a road you simply cannot pass through.

words.definition: A complete standstill in which opposing parties cannot reach any agreement.
words.example: The jury was in deadlock, split evenly, so the judge declared a mistrial.
words.mnemonic: A lock that is dead — nothing turns, nothing opens, no way forward.

words.definition: A position in which further action by either side seems impossible.
words.example: The chess game ended in a stalemate, with neither king able to move safely.
words.mnemonic: In chess your 'mate' (king) goes 'stale' — stuck with no legal move.

words.definition: A confusing and difficult problem or question with no easy answer.
words.example: How to fund the school without raising taxes was a conundrum the council debated for months.
words.mnemonic: Break it into 'con-un-drum' — a drumbeat of confusion pounding in your head.

words.definition: A person or thing that is mysterious and very hard to understand.
words.example: Even close friends found her an enigma, never sure what she truly felt.
words.mnemonic: Think of the 'Enigma' code machine — nearly impossible to decode.

words.definition: Something that blocks your way or prevents movement toward a goal.
words.example: A fallen tree was the only obstacle between us and the summit.
words.mnemonic: An 'obstacle' course is packed with walls and barriers to climb over.

words.definition: A barrier or difficulty that must be overcome in order to succeed.
words.example: Passing the bar exam was the final hurdle before she could practice law.
words.mnemonic: Picture a runner leaping a hurdle on the track — a barrier to jump.

words.definition: A state of serious or continued difficulty and misfortune.
words.example: She showed remarkable courage in the face of adversity after losing her home.
words.mnemonic: Everything turns 'adverse' — the whole world seems set against you.

words.definition: Suffering or difficulty caused by a lack of money, comfort, or safety.
words.example: The pioneers endured great hardship crossing the frozen mountains with little food.
words.mnemonic: A 'hard ship' to sail — a rough, punishing voyage through life.

words.definition: A cause of great trouble, suffering, or lasting distress.
words.example: After years of tribulation, the refugees finally found peace in a new country.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'trial' inside tribulation — a trial that tries you painfully.

words.definition: A painful or very difficult experience that tests one's endurance.
words.example: Being trapped in the elevator for six hours was an ordeal she never forgot.
words.mnemonic: 'Or-deal' — a raw deal you are forced to sit through.

words.definition: Something that causes pain, illness, or lasting suffering.
words.example: Chronic arthritis was an affliction that slowly stole his ability to paint.
words.mnemonic: Like 'inflict' — an affliction inflicts pain on the one who has it.

words.definition: A disease or disorder of the body or mind.
words.example: The doctor struggled to name the strange malady spreading through the village.
words.mnemonic: 'Mal' means bad (as in malfunction) — a malady is a bad state of health.

words.definition: A person or thing that causes great trouble or widespread suffering.
words.example: Malaria remains a scourge across much of the tropical world.
words.mnemonic: A 'scourge' was once a whip — it lashes and torments whole populations.

words.definition: Something that spoils or ruins, often spreading damage widely.
words.example: Abandoned factories were a blight on the once-thriving town.
words.mnemonic: Plant blight withers crops on sight — it rots everything it touches.

words.definition: A source of persistent harm, ruin, or great annoyance to someone.
words.example: Weeds were the bane of the gardener's carefully tended flower beds.
words.mnemonic: Bane sounds like 'pain' — and the villain Bane exists only to ruin Batman's Gotham.

words.definition: A moment of intense danger or difficulty demanding urgent decisions.
words.example: As oxygen levels dropped, the trapped crew faced a life-or-death crisis.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'krisis' = a turning point or decision — the exact instant everything must be decided.

words.definition: A disastrous event bringing great damage, distress, or misery.
words.example: The flood was a calamity that swept away entire villages overnight.
words.mnemonic: 'Call-a-medic!' — the instant disaster strikes, that's what you shout.

words.definition: A sudden event causing enormous damage, suffering, or loss.
words.example: The earthquake was a catastrophe that leveled the city in seconds.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'kata' (down) + 'strophe' (turning) = a total overturning; picture a cat knocking everything off the shelf.

words.definition: A violent, large-scale upheaval or disaster that changes everything.
words.example: The volcanic cataclysm buried the ancient town under ash and molten rock.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'kata' (down) + 'klyzein' (to wash) — a world-drowning flood washing it all away.

words.definition: A complete, humiliating failure or sudden collapse of something planned.
words.example: The product launch was a debacle, with the site crashing and refunds pouring in.
words.mnemonic: French 'débâcle' = the sudden breaking up of river ice — everything smashes apart at once.

words.definition: A total, often embarrassing failure of a plan or performance.
words.example: The surprise party turned into a fiasco when the guest of honor never showed up.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'fee-ASK-o' — you ask for your fee back after the whole thing flops.

words.definition: A state of great confusion, agitation, or disorder.
words.example: The CEO's sudden resignation threw the company into turmoil for months.
words.mnemonic: 'Turn' + 'moil' (toil) — your gut churns and toils, boiling and turning over.

words.definition: A sudden, dramatic change causing great disruption or disorder.
words.example: The revolution brought social upheaval that reshaped the entire nation.
words.mnemonic: 'Up' + 'heave' — the ground heaved violently upward, throwing everything into the air.

words.definition: Complete disorder and confusion, with no clear structure or control.
words.example: When the power failed, the crowded stadium descended into chaos.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'khaos' = the formless void before creation; hear a gaping 'chasm' swallowing all order.

words.definition: A state of disorganization, untidiness, or lack of order.
words.example: After the burglary, the entire apartment was left in complete disarray.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis-' undoes an 'array' (a neat arrangement) — so things are no longer arranged.

words.definition: To catch and twist together, or draw someone into complicated difficulties.
words.example: The dolphin became entangled in a discarded fishing net and could not surface.
words.mnemonic: 'En-' (into) + 'tangle' — to put something INTO a knotted mess, like hair caught in a comb.

words.definition: To involve someone deeply in an argument, conflict, or difficult situation.
words.example: The senator was embroiled in a bribery scandal that ended his career.
words.mnemonic: 'Em-' (in) + 'broil' — to be thrown into a boiling, heated conflict.

words.definition: To catch or trap someone, often through cunning or deception.
words.example: The con artist ensnared elderly victims with promises of huge returns.
words.mnemonic: 'En-' (into) + 'snare' — to put into a snare; picture a rabbit caught in a wire trap.

words.definition: To surround with troubles or lay siege to, causing constant harassment.
words.example: The beleaguered mayor faced protests, lawsuits, and a hostile council all at once.
words.mnemonic: From Dutch 'belegeren' (to besiege) — imagine a whole 'league' of enemies camped around your castle.

words.definition: To surround a town or fortress with armed forces to force its surrender.
words.example: For three months the army besieged the walled city until its food ran out.
words.mnemonic: Be- + siege (Latin sedere, 'to sit'): troops sit down around a castle and refuse to leave.

words.definition: To cause someone continual trouble or distress over a long period.
words.example: Technical glitches plagued the launch, crashing the app every few minutes.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'plaque' — sticky buildup on your teeth that keeps bothering you no matter how you brush.

words.definition: To annoy or trouble someone, especially in a nagging, persistent way.
words.example: The endless typos in the report vexed the meticulous editor.
words.mnemonic: Vex rhymes with 'hex' — a little curse that keeps needling and annoying you.

words.definition: To confuse someone so they cannot understand or think clearly.
words.example: The detective was perplexed by a locked room with no visible exit.
words.mnemonic: Per- (thoroughly) + plex (plectere, 'to weave'): your thoughts are thoroughly woven and tangled.

words.definition: To confuse someone completely, leaving them unable to explain or solve something.
words.example: The keys vanishing from inside a locked safe baffled everyone in the house.
words.mnemonic: Picture a 'buffalo' so puzzled it just walks in circles — baffle-lo.

words.definition: To confuse someone deeply, especially amid too many choices or unfamiliar surroundings.
words.example: The tourist stood bewildered in a maze of identical alleyways.
words.mnemonic: Be- + wilder: to be lost in the 'wild' wilderness, unsure which way to turn.

words.definition: To confuse and greatly surprise someone, or to mix two things up.
words.example: The rookie's victory confounded the critics who had predicted his defeat.
words.mnemonic: Con- (together) + found (fundere, 'to pour'): pour things together until they're hopelessly mixed.

words.definition: To block someone from reaching a goal, causing disappointment and irritation.
words.example: Heavy traffic frustrated her plan to reach the airport on time.
words.mnemonic: From Latin frustra, 'in vain' — effort spent in vain leaves you fed up.

words.definition: To irritate someone intensely until they lose all patience.
words.example: The child's endless 'why?' questions eventually exasperated the babysitter.
words.mnemonic: Ex- + asper (Latin 'rough'): someone rubs you the wrong way until you're raw with anger.

words.definition: To trouble or attack someone persistently from every side.
words.example: The expedition was beset by storms, illness, and dwindling supplies.
words.mnemonic: Be- + set: troubles are 'set' all around you, on every side at once.

words.definition: To burden or weigh down someone, making movement or progress difficult.
words.example: Encumbered by heavy backpacks, the hikers struggled up the steep trail.
words.mnemonic: En- + cumber ('a burden'): imagine a giant 'cucumber' strapped to your back, slowing you down.

words.definition: To put something at risk of harm, loss, or failure.
words.example: Skipping the safety checks could jeopardize the entire crew's lives.
words.mnemonic: Think of the show 'Jeopardy!' — every answer puts your winnings on the line.

words.definition: To put someone or something in danger.
words.example: Rising floodwaters imperiled the villages along the riverbank.
words.mnemonic: Im- (into) + peril: to place someone right into peril.

words.definition: To expose someone or something to possible harm or destruction.
words.example: Pollution endangers countless species living in the coral reef.
words.mnemonic: En- ('to make') + danger: literally to put someone into danger.

words.definition: To make something more difficult, tangled, or hard to understand.
words.example: Adding three new managers only complicated the decision-making process.
words.mnemonic: Com- (together) + plicare ('to fold'): fold many things together until it's a tangled mess.

words.definition: To help conflicting parties reach an agreement by acting as a neutral middle party.
words.example: A trusted teacher stepped in to mediate between the two feuding students.
words.mnemonic: MEDI = middle (Latin medius) — a go-between stands in the middle of a fight.

words.definition: To settle a dispute formally after hearing both sides and issuing a binding decision.
words.example: The retired judge was hired to arbitrate the contract fight between the company and its supplier.
words.mnemonic: Think 'arbiter' — the referee who makes the final call and ends the argument.

words.definition: To discuss terms with others in order to reach a mutually acceptable deal.
words.example: They spent all afternoon trying to negotiate a fair price for the used car.
words.mnemonic: NEG sounds like 'nag' — you nag back and forth until you strike a deal.

words.definition: An agreement reached when each side gives up part of what it originally wanted.
words.example: After a long argument they found a compromise: pizza one night, sushi the next.
words.mnemonic: COM (together) + PROMISE — a promise made together where everyone gives a little.

words.definition: To win over an angry or hostile person by being friendly and reasonable.
words.example: The manager tried to conciliate the upset customers with a sincere apology and a full refund.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'council' — bring people to the council table and make peace.

words.definition: To bring calm to someone by giving in to their demands or wishes.
words.example: The parents tried to appease the screaming toddler with a cookie.
words.mnemonic: aP-PEAS-e hides PEACE — hand over peace (or peas) to quiet someone down.

words.definition: To make an angry person feel calm and satisfied again.
words.example: He sent flowers to placate his girlfriend after forgetting their anniversary.
words.mnemonic: PLACATE ~ 'placid' (calm) — you turn a stormy mood placid.

words.definition: To soothe someone's anger or worry and make them less upset.
words.example: She spoke gently to mollify her frustrated coworker before the big meeting.
words.mnemonic: From Latin mollis = soft; to MOLLify is to make hard feelings soft.

words.definition: To bring peace and calm to someone or something that is upset or violent.
words.example: The nanny rocked the baby slowly to pacify her.
words.mnemonic: PACIFY ~ 'pacifier' — the plug that quiets a fussy baby; PAC = pax (peace).

words.definition: To make an unpleasant feeling less intense or painful.
words.example: A cup of tea and a few kind words helped assuage her grief.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'a-SWAGE' — a soothing salve that eases the sting away.

words.definition: To make something less extreme or harsh by adding a softening influence.
words.example: A good editor knows how to temper sharp criticism with a word of encouragement.
words.mnemonic: Like tempering steel or chocolate — controlling the heat to reach a balanced result.

words.definition: To reduce the extremeness or intensity of something.
words.example: The doctor advised him to moderate his salt intake for the sake of his heart.
words.mnemonic: MODE + RATE — keep the rate in the middle 'mode,' never at the extreme.

words.definition: To reduce tension or danger in a situation before it turns serious.
words.example: A well-timed joke helped defuse the tense standoff in the boardroom.
words.mnemonic: DE-FUSE: pull the fuse out of the bomb so it can never go off.

words.definition: To free something from knots, confusion, or a complicated situation.
words.example: It took the accountant weeks to disentangle the company's messy finances.
words.mnemonic: DIS + ENTANGLE — the direct undoing of a tangle; pick the knots apart.

words.definition: To free someone or something from a difficult or trapped situation.
words.example: She struggled to extricate her boot from the thick, sucking mud.
words.mnemonic: EX (out) + 'tricky' — get yourself out of a tricky spot.

words.definition: To set a person or group free from captivity, oppression, or control.
words.example: When the troops marched into the city, they opened the prison gates and liberated everyone held there.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'liberty' inside liberate — giving someone their liberty.

words.definition: To release someone from slavery or from legal, social, or political restrictions.
words.example: The 1863 proclamation emancipated millions who had been held as property, granting them their freedom.
words.mnemonic: 'E-man-cip' → 'a MAN is set free' from chains.

words.definition: To formally declare someone free from guilt, blame, or an obligation.
words.example: After hearing the full story, the priest absolved him, and the weight of guilt lifted from his shoulders.
words.mnemonic: 'Ab-SOLVE' — the problem of your sins is solved, wiped clean.

words.definition: To officially clear a person of blame or suspicion of wrongdoing.
words.example: New DNA evidence finally exonerated the man who had spent twelve years in prison for someone else's crime.
words.mnemonic: 'Ex-onus' — the ONUS (burden) is taken OFF you.

words.definition: To judge and declare a defendant not guilty of a crime.
words.example: The jury deliberated for an hour before returning to acquit her, and she walked out of the courtroom free.
words.mnemonic: 'A-QUIT' — the court lets you QUIT the charges and go home.

words.definition: A temporary delay or cancellation of a punishment or a difficult situation.
words.example: Minutes before the execution, the governor's call granted a reprieve, and the prisoner's sentence was put on hold.
words.mnemonic: 'RE-PRIEVE' sounds like 'relieve' — a pause that relieves the doom.

words.definition: To return to a normal state of health, strength, or function.
words.example: After a week of rest and fluids, she began to recover and was soon back on her feet.
words.mnemonic: 'RE-COVER' — you pull the covers back over yourself to get well again.

words.definition: To restore a person or thing to good health, use, or standing.
words.example: The clinic helped rehabilitate the injured athlete until he could run a full marathon again.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-HABIT' — you rebuild healthy HABITS to become whole again.

words.definition: To thoroughly examine and repair or improve a system or machine.
words.example: The mechanics took the engine completely apart to overhaul it, replacing every worn component inside.
words.mnemonic: 'OVER-HAUL' — you haul the whole thing over to the shop and redo it all.

words.definition: To make a process simpler, faster, and more efficient.
words.example: By cutting three approval steps, the manager streamlined the workflow so orders shipped in half the time.
words.mnemonic: Picture a sleek STREAM flowing in a straight LINE — no obstacles slowing it.

words.definition: To plan or invent something through careful thought.
words.example: The engineers devised a clever pulley system to lift the beams without a crane.
words.mnemonic: 'DEVISE' hides 'device' — you think up a device or scheme.

words.definition: To express or create an idea or plan in precise, systematic terms.
words.example: Before the debate, she carefully formulated each argument so every point followed logically from the last.
words.mnemonic: 'FORMULA-te' — you build it like a tidy FORMULA, step by step.

words.definition: To cleverly plan or scheme, often using trickery or artificial means.
words.example: He contrived an excuse about a sick relative so he could slip out of the meeting early.
words.mnemonic: 'CON-trive' — a CON artist schemes and tricks their way to a goal.

words.definition: To invent a story or create a mixture by combining various elements.
words.example: The children concocted a wild tale about a dragon to explain the broken vase.
words.mnemonic: 'Con-COCT' sounds like 'cook' — you cook up a story or a strange brew.

words.definition: To create or perform something spontaneously, without any prior preparation.
words.example: When the slides failed to load, the speaker simply improvised, talking the audience through the ideas from memory.
words.mnemonic: 'IM-PRO-VISE' — 'not' (im) 'provided' in advance; you make it up on the spot.
